result: {"questions":[{"question":"The placement test failed completely: 0 of 34 reference contacts were shared, and backbone RMSD was 38.6 Å against a 5 Å limit. Yet the call table says bind for all three pairs. The same program called the test pose no-bind. Does the bind call mean anything?","where":"Redocking test file (endpoint-anchor): overlap 0.0, RMSD 38.6163, 114 pose contacts, 0 shared. Call table: three rows, all bind. The aux rows set 'contacts at 4.5 Å' true for all three.","if_true":"The program's bind label is only physical contact somewhere on the surface, not binding at the published site. A bind call is then nearly guaranteed. The call table, scores and site classes would not separate binders from non-binders.","changes":"The design assumes redocking can reproduce a known site, and that bind and no-bind calls are meaningful. If calls carry no information, the timing inputs measure the cost of producing labels that do not discriminate."},{"question":"Is the docking setup too weak to find any site? It used 2 swarms, 20 glowworms (search agents) and 20 steps, with no restraint to the published interface. Would a larger search find the right site, and how much longer would it take?","where":"Docking parameters in the redocking and aux rows: swarms 2, glowworms 20, steps 20, restrained false. The redocking took 25.9 s serial and 19.4 s on 4 cores.","if_true":"The 38.6 Å miss comes from a toy search, not from a method limit. The auxiliary time of about 0.009 h per pair would also be a toy figure. A real docking pass would cost much more.","changes":"The failed gate would say nothing about whether the method works, so every input's void or fail would be uninformative. The design never states a search size that justifies running the test at all."},{"question":"The auxiliary time per pair is 0.00907, 0.00949 and 0.00992 hours, mean 0.0095 h. That is about 35 times below the lower edge of 0.3333 h, and about 105 times below the card's 1 h. Does this measure the card's auxiliary work or only a 22-second toy docking?","where":"Auxiliary rows (hours field) and the endpoint for auxiliary hours per pair (decision FAIL, valid true). Docking took 22.2, 22.5 and 22.9 s of 32.6, 34.2 and 35.7 s total.","if_true":"The FAIL is real only for this stand-in. It shows the card's 1 h guess is far too high only if the card's work matches. The design's own reading of 'auxiliary' was a guess. The FAIL is also the only decided input after a failed gate that should have halted the run.","changes":"The hypothesis says each input holds in its band. A decided FAIL here would refute input 3. But the design said a gate miss means no input is reported as measured. Is the FAIL valid, or should it be void?"},{"question":"Is the three-pair stand-in really three different pairs? Every receptor sequence is identical. Each capsid is the same 517-residue chain A from 6IHB, plus a second copy of chain A cut to 169, 259 or 349 residues and shifted 60 Å. Is that a capsid?","where":"Pairs file: lengths 517+169+94=780, 517+259+94=870, 517+349+94=960. Both capsid pieces have source chain A. All three receptor sequences are equal.","if_true":"The pairs differ only in length of a duplicated fragment. Timing and call spread across them says little about three real capsids. A 'capsid' of one crystal chain and a shifted copy has no real three-fold axis.","changes":"The design treats three pairs, one per capsid, as a sample of nine. If they are synthetic fragments, no input transfers to the card's protocol. The distance to the nearest three-fold axis (57.1, 66.8, 64.8 Å) is then also meaningless."},{"question":"The molecular dynamics systems held 706,477, 1,157,381 and 1,136,222 atoms. About 1,372 s went to building three systems that could never count. The design assumes the described system size is reachable with these stand-ins."},{"question":"Only 1 of 9 planned AlphaFold timings ran.
